questions.q: Empirical risk minimization returns $h_S=\arg\min_{h\in\mathcal{H}}\widehat R(h)$. Why can $\widehat R(h_S)$ be a badly optimistic estimate of $R(h_S)$?
choices: Because $\widehat R$ uses the wrong loss function
Because $h_S$ is selected using the same sample on which $\widehat R$ is evaluated, biasing it downward
Because the law of large numbers does not apply to averages of losses
questions.explain: For a single fixed $h$, $\widehat R(h)$ is unbiased for $R(h)$. But $h_S$ is chosen to minimize the empirical risk on the very same data, so $\widehat R(h_S)$ is biased low — this selection effect is exactly what uniform convergence over $\mathcal{H}$ is needed to control.

questions.q: Under $0$–$1$ loss for binary classification with $\eta(x)=\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X=x)$, the Bayes-optimal predictor is:
choices: $h^\star(x)=\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]$ rounded to the nearest training label
questions.explain: The Bayes classifier predicts the more likely label: $\mathbf{1}[\eta(x)\ge\tfrac12]$. Its risk is the irreducible Bayes risk $R^\star$. The regression function $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X=x]=\eta(x)$ is Bayes-optimal for squared loss, not $0$–$1$ loss.

questions.q: The excess risk $R(h_S)-R^\star$ splits into estimation error and approximation error. Select every statement that is correct.
choices: Enlarging $\mathcal{H}$ tends to decrease approximation error
Enlarging $\mathcal{H}$ tends to decrease estimation error
Approximation error is $R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})-R^\star$, the gap between the best-in-class and the Bayes risk
Estimation error is $R(h_S)-R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})$, the cost of learning from a finite sample
questions.explain: A richer class lowers approximation error (it can represent more) but raises estimation error (more ways to overfit a finite sample). Approximation error $=R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})-R^\star$ and estimation error $=R(h_S)-R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})$; option 2 has the wrong direction for estimation error.

questions.q: Realizable PAC with a finite class: using $m\ge\frac1\varepsilon\big(\ln|\mathcal{H}|+\ln\frac1\delta\big)$, how many samples suffice for $|\mathcal{H}|=e^{10}$, $\varepsilon=0.1$, $\delta=e^{-2}$? (Report the bound rounded to the nearest integer.)
Hoeffding's inequality bounds $\mathbb{P}(|\frac1m\sum Z_i-\mu|>t)$ for i.i.d. $Z_i\in[0,1]$ by:
questions.explain: Hoeffding gives the sub-Gaussian tail $2e^{-2mt^2}$ for bounded summands — no variance estimate needed. Applied to losses $\ell(h(x_i),y_i)\in[0,1]$, $\widehat R(h)$ concentrates around $R(h)$ at deviation scale $1/\sqrt m$.

questions.q: Why does the agnostic finite-class sample complexity scale as $1/\varepsilon^2$ while the realizable one scales as $1/\varepsilon$?
choices: Agnostic learning needs a two-sided Hoeffding bound at level $\varepsilon/2$, whose exponent $e^{-m\varepsilon^2/2}$ forces $m\propto 1/\varepsilon^2$
Realizable learning uses a larger hypothesis class
Agnostic learning ignores the union bound
The realizable bound is simply loose by a factor of $1/\varepsilon$
questions.explain: In the realizable case only consistent hypotheses ($\widehat R=0$) survive, giving a one-sided multiplicative-Chernoff rate $\propto 1/\varepsilon$. The agnostic case must control two-sided deviations of magnitude $\varepsilon/2$, and Hoeffding's $e^{-m\varepsilon^2/2}$ forces $m\propto 1/\varepsilon^2$ — the price of label noise.

questions.q: What is the VC dimension of the class of half-planes (affine threshold classifiers) in $\mathbb{R}^2$?
questions.explain: Half-planes in $\mathbb{R}^d$ have VC dimension $d+1$, so $d=2$ gives $3$. Three points in general position are shattered (all $8$ labelings are linearly separable), but no $4$ points can be — e.g. the XOR labeling of a square is not linearly separable.

questions.q: The Sauer–Shelah lemma states that if $\mathrm{VC}(\mathcal{H})=d<\infty$ then for $m\ge d$:
questions.explain: Finite VC dimension forces the growth function from exponential ($2^m$) down to a degree-$d$ polynomial: $\Pi_{\mathcal{H}}(m)\le\sum_{i\le d}\binom{m}{i}\le(em/d)^d$. This polynomial bound is what makes infinite classes learnable, replacing $\ln|\mathcal{H}|$ by $\approx d\ln(em/d)$.

questions.q: Match each concept class to its VC dimension.
questions.explain: Thresholds shatter 1 point but not 2 (can't realize $(1,0)$ left-to-right): VC 1. Intervals shatter 2 but not 3 (can't realize $1,0,1$): VC 2. Axis-aligned rectangles shatter 4 points but not 5: VC 4. Half-planes in $\mathbb{R}^d$: VC $d+1$.

questions.q: As the sample size $m$ grows with the VC dimension $d$ held fixed, the VC generalization bound $O\!\big(\sqrt{(d\ln(m/d)+\ln(1/\delta))/m}\big)$ behaves like:
choices: $\Theta(\sqrt{d/m})$ up to a $\sqrt{\ln m}$ factor — it tends to $0$
questions.explain: The dominant term is $\sqrt{d\ln(m/d)/m}\to 0$ as $m\to\infty$: the bound decays essentially like $\sqrt{d/m}$ (with a mild logarithmic factor). More data tightens it; more capacity $d$ loosens it.

questions.q: By the Fundamental Theorem of Statistical Learning (binary classes, $0$–$1$ loss), which of the following are equivalent to '$\mathcal{H}$ has finite VC dimension'?
choices: Every ERM rule is a successful learner for $\mathcal{H}$
questions.explain: The theorem chains finite VC dimension $\iff$ uniform convergence $\iff$ (agnostic and realizable) PAC-learnability $\iff$ ERM succeeds. Finiteness of $\mathcal{H}$ is sufficient but not necessary — half-planes are infinite yet have VC dimension $d+1$.

questions.q: Uniform convergence ($\sup_h|R(h)-\widehat R(h)|\le\varepsilon$) implies that ERM's output $h_S$ satisfies:
questions.explain: Chaining: $R(h_S)\le\widehat R(h_S)+\varepsilon\le\widehat R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})+\varepsilon\le R(h^\star_{\mathcal{H}})+2\varepsilon$. The middle step uses that $h_S$ minimizes empirical risk; the outer two use uniform convergence applied to $h_S$ and to $h^\star_{\mathcal{H}}$.

questions.q: For the class of ALL $\pm1$-valued functions on $m$ fixed points, what is the empirical Rademacher complexity $\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_S=\mathbb{E}_\sigma[\sup_h\frac1m\sum_i\sigma_i h(x_i)]$?
questions.explain: The class realizes every sign pattern, so for any $\sigma$ we pick $h(x_i)=\sigma_i$, giving $\frac1m\sum\sigma_i^2=\frac1m\sum 1=1$. Hence $\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_S=1$ — maximal capacity. A class that fits arbitrary noise perfectly cannot generalize.

questions.q: In the Rademacher bound $R(h)\le\widehat R(h)+2\,\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_S(\ell\circ\mathcal{H})+3\sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2m)}$, where does the leading factor of $2$ come from?
choices: From the two-sided nature of the loss
From the symmetrization (ghost-sample) step that introduces the Rademacher signs
From the union bound over two hypotheses
From the variance being at most $1/2$
questions.explain: The $2$ is the symmetrization constant: bounding $\mathbb{E}\sup_h(R-\widehat R)$ by introducing an independent ghost sample and Rademacher signs costs a factor of $2$ in front of $\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_S$. McDiarmid then converts the expectation bound into a high-probability bound, contributing the $\sqrt{\ln(2/\delta)/(2m)}$ term.

questions.q: Margin-based bounds for $\|w\|\le B$ linear classifiers on $\|x\|\le R$ data generalize at rate $\tilde O\!\big(BR/(\gamma\sqrt m)\big)$ for margin $\gamma$. The striking feature is that this rate is:
choices: Independent of the ambient dimension — only $B$, $R$, $\gamma$, $m$ enter
Proportional to the number of support vectors squared
questions.explain: Because $\widehat{\mathfrak{R}}_S$ of the norm-bounded linear class is $\le BR/\sqrt m$ (Cauchy–Schwarz + Jensen), the bound has no explicit dependence on dimension. This dimension-freeness is exactly why large-margin SVMs and boosting generalize despite enormous parameter counts.

questions.q: In the squared-error decomposition $\mathbb{E}_S[(\hat f_S(x)-y)^2]=\text{bias}^2+\text{variance}+\sigma^2$, which term does a richer (more flexible) model class primarily reduce?
questions.explain: A more flexible class can approximate $f$ more closely, lowering bias — but it is more sensitive to the particular sample, raising variance. The noise $\sigma^2$ is irreducible (the Bayes floor). The optimal complexity sits at the bottom of the resulting U-shaped total error.

questions.q: Which property distinguishes lasso ($\ell_1$) regularization from ridge ($\ell_2$)?
choices: Lasso's constraint region has corners on the axes, so it drives some coefficients exactly to zero — producing sparse models
Ridge produces sparse models while lasso does not
questions.explain: The $\ell_1$ ball is a cross-polytope with vertices on the coordinate axes; the constrained optimum often lands on a corner, zeroing out coefficients (variable selection). Ridge's $\ell_2$ ball is smooth, so it shrinks all coefficients toward $0$ but rarely sets any exactly to $0$.

questions.q: Structural risk minimization chooses among nested classes $\mathcal{H}_1\subset\mathcal{H}_2\subset\cdots$ by minimizing:
choices: Empirical risk alone, over the largest class
Empirical risk plus a capacity penalty $\mathrm{pen}(d_k,m,\delta)$, balancing fit against complexity
The training accuracy on a single held-out point
questions.explain: SRM minimizes the guaranteed risk — empirical risk plus the complexity penalty from the uniform-convergence bound. This automates the choice of capacity, formalizing the U-curve's minimum: large classes fit better but pay a bigger penalty.
